title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate the retrieval and citation behavior of AI chatbots by seeding the web with fabricated academic-style content. A non-existent organization published a large volume of material formatted to resemble research reports, on a platform specifically designed to make AI systems treat that content as citable. The failure mode is not one inside the AI itself but upstream of it: AI systems that draw on web content have no reliable mechanism to verify whether a source institution actually exists or whether its output was produced to influence the system rather than inform it.

The operation was registered as foreign propaganda work with the U.S. Justice Department, so its nature as an influence effort is on record, but registration does not establish the full extent of its effect on AI outputs. It is not established how many AI systems ingested and repeated the material, nor what harm, if any, resulted from those outputs.

What the incident illustrates is a structural gap in AI deployment: systems that synthesize and present information without citing sources cannot easily be audited for the provenance of the claims they make, and content engineered specifically to exploit that gap is difficult to distinguish from genuine research at the point of ingestion.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded organization called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, which does not legally exist, created a fake research website to influence artificial intelligence chatbots toward pro-Israel messaging. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words, formatted as academic research with questions designed to be searched in chatbots. The reports addressed controversial topics like alleged Israeli war crimes and genocide claims in Gaza, consistently framing information to minimize criticism of Israel. The operation was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign propaganda work and used a specialized platform designed to optimize content for AI systems to cite it.

This effort represents part of a broader campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through international companies including Havas Media. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the expensive public relations campaign has failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, which has significantly declined since 2022. Researchers warn that this represents a new threat to information reliability, as AI systems trained on such material will spread narratives without citing sources, making fact-checking impossible.
